Right ankle of a 25-year-old woman with painful posteromedial swelling. MRI c–f marks the accessory soleus belly and local course; coronal T1 panel f marks a muscular insertion on the medial calcaneus. Clinical photograph a and lateral radiograph b provide separate context and are not credited as MRI. Identified in this figure: Accessory soleus: labelled belly and limited visible course; Accessory soleus: local muscular distal insertion at the medial calcaneus. Identified in clinical photograph panels (a): Posteromedial right ankle swelling during plantar flexion. External photograph only; does not show the internal muscle course or an MRI signal. Identified in radiography panels (b): Obliterated Kager fat pad in a lateral right ankle radiograph. Projection context only; does not establish the muscle or tendon signal on MRI. Published sections do not establish the complete proximal attachment, full distal footprint, physical tissue dimensions, dynamic compression or a 3D volume. The source cases are symptomatic, not normal-reference examinations. Published PDF panels are retained at their 300 dpi placement. Original DICOM acquisition metadata and a higher-resolution prepublication master remain unverified. © 2020 Mihovil Plečko, Igor Knežević, Damjan Dimnjaković, Mario Josipović and Ivan Bojanić. Accessory Soleus Muscle: Two Case Reports with a Completely Different Presentation Caused by the Same Entity. Case Reports in Orthopedics 2020:8851920, DOI 10.1155/2020/8851920. CC BY 4.0. Complete Figure 1 rendered from the published PDF to PNG, preserving original annotations and layout. No endorsement implied. Source: NLM/PMC Article Datasets, retrieved 30 September 2026. This snapshot may not reflect the latest NLM data. No NLM endorsement is implied. Source article Original figure CC BY 4.0

Right ankle of a 31-year-old woman with pain and plantar paresthesia; the case report documents concomitant tarsal tunnel syndrome. MRI b–f marks the accessory soleus and its tendinous distal insertion. Radiograph a is separate projection context. The source calls f axial, but its displayed anatomy appears longitudinal; that panel’s exact plane remains unresolved. Identified in this figure: Accessory soleus: labelled belly and limited visible course; Accessory soleus: local tendinous distal insertion at the medial calcaneus. Identified in radiography panels (a): Lateral right ankle projection with Kager fat-pad obliteration and calcaneal insula compacta. Radiography only; not credited as MRI or as proof of nerve compression. Published sections do not establish the complete proximal attachment, full distal footprint, physical tissue dimensions, dynamic compression or a 3D volume. The source cases are symptomatic, not normal-reference examinations. Published PDF panels are retained at their 300 dpi placement. Original DICOM acquisition metadata and a higher-resolution prepublication master remain unverified. Figure 3f has an unresolved source-caption/visual-plane discrepancy. © 2020 Mihovil Plečko, Igor Knežević, Damjan Dimnjaković, Mario Josipović and Ivan Bojanić. Single transverse ankle MRI from a 34-year-old man with left posterior ankle pain and a prominent posterior talar process. The white arrow marks the source-identified accessory muscle near the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle. The article identifies FDAL during subsequent endoscopy. This section does not establish its full course, attachments or symptom causation. Identified in this figure: FDAL accessory muscle: source-labelled local cross-section. A local muscle cross-section only. MRI sequence, voxel spacing and full scan coverage are unreported. This is a symptomatic posterior-ankle case, not a normal ankle or a demonstrated tarsal-tunnel compression example. No origin, insertion footprint, physical dimensions or 3D geometry is supplied. © 2015 Jorge Pablo Batista, Jorge Javier del Vecchio, Pau Golanó and Jordi Vega. Flexor Digitorum Accessorius Longus: Importance of Posterior Ankle Endoscopy. Case Reports in Orthopedics 2015:823107, DOI 10.1155/2015/823107. CC BY 3.0. Complete Figure 2 rendered at the PDF image’s 600 dpi placement to lossless PNG, preserving its white arrow and scale markings. No endorsement implied. Source: NLM/PMC Article Datasets, retrieved 30 September 2026. This snapshot may not reflect the latest NLM data. No NLM endorsement is implied. Source article Original figure CC BY 3.0

One source-depicted peroneus-quartus pattern alongside the usual brevis/longus tendons. It is a teaching course illustration, not a measured subject or a universal origin/insertion map. Identified in this figure: Peroneus quartus: source-depicted local course; Peroneus brevis; Peroneus longus; Retrotrochlear eminence of calcaneus. One source-described PQ pattern only. Other origins and insertions occur; no measured tissue dimensions, complete individual attachment footprint, dynamic compression or 3D volume is supplied. The PDF contains more pixels than the repository preview; this does not establish original scan resolution or anatomical accuracy. Article © 2025 Yavuz Yuksel, Tarkan Ergun and Ozkan Kose. Prevalence of the Peroneus Quartus Muscle and Its Association with Peroneal Tendon Pathologies: An MRI Study of 1160 Ankles. Diagnostics 15(18):2329, DOI 10.3390/diagnostics15182329. CC BY 4.0. Original Figure 1 illustration signed Eylem 2025; creator credit/signature retained. Complete Figure 1 rendered from the published PDF to PNG, preserving original annotations and layout. No endorsement implied. Source: NLM/PMC Article Datasets, retrieved 30 September 2026. This snapshot may not reflect the latest NLM data. No NLM endorsement is implied. Source article Original figure CC BY 4.0

Peroneus quartus is present in this source variant example. Panel a is axial fat-suppressed proton-density FSE MRI; blue, green and red arrows identify peroneus brevis, peroneus longus and peroneus quartus, with yellow arrows marking the accessory belly. Coronal T1 FSE b and sagittal T1 FSE c show its visible descent toward the calcaneus. Side and individual clinical status are unreported; this example does not establish a complete course or attachment footprint. Identified in this figure: Peroneus quartus (source-labelled accessory belly and limited visible descent); Peroneus brevis (source-labelled local axial appearance); Peroneus longus (source-labelled local axial appearance). Source-labelled peroneus quartus variant in three published sections. No side, individual age/sex, complete exam findings or global normality is supplied. The study uses 1.5 T MRI, but this figure has no DICOM metadata or exact panel-specific acquisition provenance. The published figure cannot establish a full musculotendinous course, attachment footprint, tissue dimensions, dynamic crowding or symptom causation; no 3D reconstruction is supported. The caption specifies a distal direction toward the retrotrochlear eminence, which is not equivalent to a validated attachment footprint. Its case-specific location is not a universal origin/insertion pattern. No accessory soleus or FDAL is illustrated. The PDF contains more pixels than the repository preview; this does not establish original scan resolution or anatomical accuracy. © 2025 Yavuz Yuksel, Tarkan Ergun and Ozkan Kose. Prevalence of the Peroneus Quartus Muscle and Its Association with Peroneal Tendon Pathologies: An MRI Study of 1160 Ankles. Diagnostics 15(18):2329, DOI 10.3390/diagnostics15182329. CC BY 4.0. Complete Figure 2 rendered from the published PDF to PNG, preserving original annotations and layout. No endorsement implied. Source: NLM/PMC Article Datasets, retrieved 30 September 2026. This snapshot may not reflect the latest NLM data. No NLM endorsement is implied. Source article Original figure CC BY 4.0
